newsitem.title: GERMANY: German minister meets angry anti-nuclear activists.
newsitem.headline: German minister meets angry anti-nuclear activists.

text.p: Environment Minister Angela Merkel on Wednesday met anti-nuclear activists to try to ease tension over the arrival of a shipment of nuclear waste to a north German dump which has sparked fierce protests.

Around 250 demonstrators waving placards reading "Piss off nuclear waste!" and "Merkel, life will punish those who come too late" scuffled with police as Merkel arrived in the northern town of Luechow.
Merkel was due to meet representatives of a local action group, the church, police and the local community and said she hoped both sides would not stick to their hostile positions.

The anti-nuclear protest has heated up ahead of a shipment of nuclear waste due to arrive sometime in the next week at the medium-term nuclear storage site at Gorleben, east of Hanover, a favourite target of campaigners.
In recent weeks, suspected activists have sabotaged rail lines, smashed windows of public buildings in Hamburg and daubed walls with anti-nuclear slogans.
In a sign of widespread local opposition, hundreds of children have occupied school halls in the area to stop them being used to house police drafted in to guard the shipment.

Last year more than 19,000 police and border guards joined the biggest security operation in German peacetime history to get a shipment to the plant and police and politicians fear a repeat of mass demonstrations.

Merkel said before meeting the activists there was no alternative to transporting nuclear waste to medium term dumps like Gorleben and nothing to be gained from shipping it to other plants like La Hague in France or Sellafield in England.
"Sticking your head in the sand and saying 'to France!' is no solution," she said.
But the head of the German police union, Gerhard Vogler, said this kind of nuclear waste transport was "too dangerous, too expensive and possibly unnecessary".
He said although it had not been proven, police guarding the shipment could still be affected by radiation.

The environmental group Greenpeace, which is planning protests against the shipment, said rail workers, police, demonstrators and journalists likely to come close to the waste could all be at risk from radiation.

"Merkel should investigate the dangers of the shipment, rather than justifying her energy policies by talking to the citizens of Gorleben," Greenpeace nuclear expert Helmut Hirsch said in a statement.
But a spokesman for the Federal Office for Radiation Protection, Eckart Viel, said the population was not at risk from radiation, even if there was a serious accident.
The latest delivery will include two rail containers from France and four more from German power plants, being moved together to save costs for the required security operation.
Merkel said the federal government would not contribute to the costs of policing the route of the shipment, currently being met by the northern state of Lower Saxony.

The state's interior minister, Gerhard Glogowski, warned the security operation would cost more than an original estimate of 66 million marks ($40 million) and said it was absurd Lower Saxony had to carry these costs.

Lower Saxony has complained to the Federal Constitutional Court and wants the government to meet future shipment costs. Glogowski said he would make sure the shipment went smoothly, despite his personal opposition to nuclear energy. ($ = 1.670 German Marks)
